title: Sundubu Jjigae
subtitle: Korean soft tofu stew with pork and chilli
excerpt: Sundubu jjigae is a Korean stew built around soft, silken tofu. It has a deep red broth from gochugaru chilli flakes and is bubbling hot when it arrives at the table. The stew is quick to make and deeply satisfying on cold days.
sourceNotes: Sundubu jjigae is one of Korea's most popular stews. Sundubu means uncurdled, freshly made soft tofu. The stew is served in a heated earthenware pot (dolsot) so it is still boiling when it reaches the table. Korean restaurants in the US helped popularise it internationally from the 1980s onward.

content.text: Sundubu jjigae is one of the fastest Korean stews to make. The key is silken tofu -- do not press or drain it. It breaks apart gently in the broth, which is exactly what you want. Crack an egg in at the end and let it poach in the residual heat while the stew sits on the table.

items.prepNote: use 300g soft silken tofu -- do not press or drain it
use Korean gochugaru chilli flakes if available -- they give the distinctive red colour
crack one raw egg into the stew at the end -- let it poach in the heat

content.text: Heat the oil in a saucepan over medium heat. Add the garlic and chilli flakes. Stir for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the pork mince. Cook for 3 to 4 minutes, breaking it up with a spoon.
Add the mushrooms and spring onion. Stir for 1 minute.
Pour in the stock and soy sauce. Bring to a boil.
Add the soft tofu in spoonfuls -- it will break apart slightly, which is fine. Simmer for 5 minutes.
Crack a raw egg into the stew. Leave it to poach for 1 to 2 minutes until the white is just set. Serve immediately in the cooking pot with steamed rice.

items.symptom: Stew is not red or spicy enough
items.fix: The red colour comes from Korean gochugaru chilli flakes. Regular chilli flakes work but the colour and flavour are different. Add more in small amounts -- the heat builds quickly in a hot liquid.

content.text: Sundubu jjigae is served in a bubbling earthenware pot in Korean restaurants. The raw egg cracked in at the end is a signature detail. It poaches gently in the residual heat. The stew is eaten with rice and a selection of small side dishes (banchan). It is warming, hearty, and very quick to make.
